title: A new wave of sutras
hookLine: new scriptures appear, centered on the bodhisattva who waits to free all beings

cards: A sutra opens the way the old ones do: thus have I heard. The Buddha is seated among his followers. But the crowd is different.
Alongside the monks sit beings called bodhisattvas, whole assemblies of them, and the teaching that follows sounds new.
In India, texts like this began to circulate: the Perfection of Wisdom sutras, the Lotus Sutra, and others. The communities that treasured them gave their way a name. Mahayana.

teach.b: First, the figure at the center. A bodhisattva is a being set on full awakening.
The word isn't new: we met the bodhisatta in the Jataka tales, the Buddha in his earlier lives, and the Theravada tradition honors that path too.
What the new sutras do is hold it up as a path for many to walk, not only the one who became the Buddha. Second, the vow.

teach.h: THE VOW: FOR THE SAKE OF ALL BEINGS.
teach.b: In these texts the bodhisattva sets out to awaken not for themselves alone but for the sake of all beings.
One popular way of putting it: the bodhisattva waits at the threshold of nibbana until every being can pass through.
Some Mahayana teachers put it differently: not waiting, but working, life after life, until all are free. Either way, the heart of it is three words. For all beings.

Third, a twist. The Diamond Sutra, one of the Perfection of Wisdom texts, has the Buddha say that a bodhisattva should resolve to lead all beings to nibbana, and yet hold that no being at all has been led there.
If he thinks of a self, a being, a person, he is no bodhisattva.

teach.h: HELP ALL, AND BUILD NO SELF FROM IT.
teach.b: It echoes Nagasena's chariot, turned toward compassion: help everyone, and build no self out of the helping. Fourth, where the texts came from.
Followers of these sutras received them as the Buddha's word.

A story some tell says certain texts were kept by the nagas, serpent beings, until the right teacher came for them. Historians say simply that these texts appear later than the older collections. Both views are held.

how: In Mahayana communities, sutras such as the Heart Sutra, the Diamond Sutra and the Lotus Sutra are chanted and studied, and the bodhisattva vow, to seek awakening for the sake of all beings, is taken in ceremony.

o: the old canon in Pali, kept by the elders
a king's council that closed the canon
the great vehicle, the way of the new sutras

for the sake of all beings

s: the bodhisattva idea appears only in Mahayana
the Jataka tales tell of the bodhisatta's earlier lives, and Theravada honors that path too.
all Mahayana teachers describe the bodhisattva as waiting at the threshold
some put it as working, life after life, until all are free.
the Diamond Sutra warns against building a self out of helping
a bodhisattva who thinks of a self, a being or a person is no bodhisattva.

games.q: you're a bodhisattva in the new sutras. you've resolved to awaken. for whose sake?
o: your own, first; others can follow.
games.why: the vow is for the sake of all beings. and the Diamond Sutra adds a twist: lead them all, yet hold that no being has been led.

practice: Think of someone who waits for others, the friend who walks at the slow one's pace, the parent who eats last, the coworker who stays until everyone's file is in, and stay with that face, noticing what their waiting gives.
Then gently widen the circle, to the people around them and the people around those, as far as it will grow.

wordCard.voice: Mahayana. The great vehicle: the name taken by communities following the new sutras, with the bodhisattva and the vow for all beings at their center.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the great vehicle, the name the followers of the new sutras gave their way.

carryVoice: Your line: for all beings. Awakening sought not for yourself alone, but for everyone. Until tomorrow.
